modules.summary: Qualify complex international claims with hedging language and maintain an objective tone using impersonal structures.

grammar.name: Hedging language
grammar.explanation: Hedging shows how confident you are, protects you from overclaiming and makes debate sound reasonable rather than dogmatic.
keyPoints: It appears that the data supports the claim, although further study is needed.
This may suggest a link between the two, rather than prove one.
Use tend to, arguably, to some extent and it is likely that to soften claims.
grammar.example: The figures appear to support the tax, although they may also reflect a broader change in buying habits.

items.prompt: Which sentence is best hedged for an academic essay?
options: The evidence suggests that sugar taxes tend to reduce consumption.
items.answer: The evidence suggests that sugar taxes tend to reduce consumption.
items.explanation: Suggests and tend to signal limited confidence without weakening the point.

items.prompt: This ___ suggest a link, but it does not prove one.
items.explanation: May expresses possibility and keeps the claim proportionate.

items.prompt: Which phrase overclaims?
items.explanation: Beyond doubt is an absolute claim, the opposite of hedging.

grammar.name: Impersonal structures
grammar.explanation: Create formal distance in policy essays and position statements with "It appears that…", "There seems to be…", and "One could argue that…".
keyPoints: Replace "I think everybody knows" with "It is widely acknowledged that…".
Use "There tends to be…" or "There appears to be…" to introduce patterns neutrally.
Pair impersonal frames with modals (may, could, might) to avoid sounding dogmatic.
grammar.example: It appears that cross-border river treaties tend to endure when local farmers are consulted early.

items.prompt: ___ seems to be growing agreement that regional water sharing prevents disputes.
items.explanation: "There seems to be + noun phrase" is a natural impersonal structure.

items.prompt: It is ___ acknowledged that preventive disaster aid costs far less than rebuilding.
items.explanation: Adverb "widely" modifies the participle "acknowledged".

items.prompt: Which opening best fits a balanced B2 position statement?
options: Everyone knows global treaties always fail completely.
One could argue that international agreements work best when targets are verifiable.
International agreements are totally useless in every case.
items.answer: One could argue that international agreements work best when targets are verifiable.
items.explanation: Combines an impersonal frame with measured qualification.

inputs.title: Shared rivers, shared futures
inputs.body: Rachel: Global challenges like water scarcity rarely stop at national borders, yet international treaties often take years to negotiate. Vikram, you advise municipal water boards on cross-border river basins. Why do some multilateral water agreements endure for decades while others stall? Vikram: It appears that successful treaties share two quiet features. First, they allocate technical monitoring to joint engineering teams who exchange rainfall data weekly, even when politicians disagree. Second, they build flexibility into dry years instead of locking countries into rigid quotas. Look at how upstream reservoirs and downstream irrigation districts work when they share real-time satellite readings: farmers gain weeks of warning before a drought deepens. Rachel: Critics sometimes argue that international frameworks have no teeth—that governments ignore voluntary targets whenever domestic pressure rises. Vikram: That is a fair concern, and voluntary pledges alone certainly tend to fall short. However, linking cross-border cooperation to shared infrastructure grants creates a practical incentive to stay at the table. When neighbouring cities co-fund flood barriers and early-warning sensors, building resilience becomes mutually rewarding rather than a zero-sum contest. One could argue that steady, modest cooperation saves far more livelihoods than dramatic summit speeches.

questions.prompt: What helps multilateral river agreements survive political disagreements?
options: Weekly technical data sharing and flexible drought rules
Waiting for summit speeches once every ten years
questions.answer: Weekly technical data sharing and flexible drought rules

questions.prompt: How can agreements overcome the weakness of purely voluntary pledges?
options: By tying cooperation to shared infrastructure funding and incentives
By using rigid quotas regardless of rainfall
questions.answer: By tying cooperation to shared infrastructure funding and incentives

inputs.title: Why local cities are quietly shaping global climate action
inputs.body: Public attention during international climate summits naturally centres on prime ministers, binding treaties, and national carbon pledges. Yet a growing body of policy research suggests that many of the fastest reductions in emissions and energy waste happen far closer to the ground—inside city halls, port authorities, and regional power grids. Because mayors manage buses, building codes, waste collection, and urban tree canopies directly, municipal networks can test practical ideas without waiting years for every national legislature to agree. Through multilateral city alliances, engineers in Medellín, Rotterdam, and Bristol exchange exact blueprints for sponge parks, district heating, and flood resilience. Of course, cities cannot solve global disparities on their own. National governments still control tax policy, cross-border energy grids, and humanitarian aid budgets, and smaller towns often lack the specialist staff needed to clear funding bottlenecks. It is widely acknowledged, therefore, that global cooperation works best as a two-way partnership: treaties set ambitious rules and allocate finance fairly, while local municipalities turn broad commitments into streets people actually experience. Measured optimism, grounded in transparent data rather than slogans, tends to sustain public support longest. Equally encouraging is how university researchers, patient networks, and coastal municipalities now share open-source tools across continents. Rather than guarding every flood map or agricultural forecast behind expensive licences, public consortia publish translated manuals and low-cost sensor designs that smaller regions can adapt immediately. Of course, shared tools alone cannot replace steady finance or fair trade rules, and rich nations still face rightful scrutiny over whether promised adaptation funds arrive on schedule. Even so, practical technical solidarity demonstrates that global cooperation need not wait for unanimous treaties before protecting vulnerable communities on the ground.

questions.prompt: Why can municipal networks sometimes test climate solutions faster than national governments?
options: Mayors directly manage buses, building codes, and local services
Cities do not need any public funding
questions.answer: Mayors directly manage buses, building codes, and local services

questions.prompt: What bottleneck do smaller towns often face according to the brief?
options: A shortage of specialist staff to navigate funding rules
questions.answer: A shortage of specialist staff to navigate funding rules

modules.title: Innovation and the future
modules.summary: Project future milestones accurately with future perfect and future continuous, and calibrate probability with B2 speculation language.

grammar.name: Future perfect and future continuous
grammar.explanation: Use future continuous (will be + -ing) for an action in progress at a future moment, and future perfect (will have + past participle) for an achievement completed before a future deadline.
keyPoints: By 2035, coastal regions will have replaced most diesel ferries with electric vessels.
This time next decade, far more technicians will be maintaining battery storage grids.
Pair future perfect with "by + future time" (by 2030, by the end of the decade).
grammar.example: By 2032, engineers will have installed smart meters across the district and hospitals will be running on microgrids.

items.prompt: By the end of the decade, rural clinics ___ shifted most routine bookings online.
items.explanation: "By + future time" calls for future perfect ("will have + past participle").

items.prompt: Five years from now, commuters ___ using unified smart tickets across regions.
items.explanation: Action in progress at a future point uses future continuous ("will be + -ing").

items.prompt: By 2040, how many countries ___ phased out coal power completely?
items.explanation: Completion before 2040 uses future perfect.

grammar.name: Speculation language
grammar.explanation: Express nuanced degrees of likelihood about emerging technologies using "is bound to", "is likely/unlikely to", "may well", and "there is every chance that".
keyPoints: High certainty: Solid-state batteries are bound to cut charging times.
Moderate probability: Routine diagnostic tools may well save nurses hours of paperwork.
Low probability: Driverless lorries are unlikely to replace local delivery drivers overnight.
grammar.example: Automated translation tools may well speed up travel bookings, though face-to-face diplomacy is bound to stay human.

items.prompt: With battery costs falling steadily, home solar storage ___ become far more common.
items.explanation: "Be bound to + infinitive" expresses strong future likelihood.

items.prompt: Early prototypes ___ fail in real winter conditions before engineers refine them.
items.explanation: "May well + bare infinitive" expresses realistic possibility.

items.prompt: Full-scale fusion power is ___ to replace wind farms before 2035.
items.explanation: "Be unlikely to + infinitive" expresses low probability politely.

inputs.title: Forecasting 2035: hype vs. quiet breakthroughs
inputs.body: Nora: Every January brings bold predictions about flying taxis and robotic households. Yet looking back twenty years, the innovations that genuinely reshaped daily life were often quieter: pocket maps, lithium batteries, and instant video calls. Devon, what separates lasting breakthroughs from flashy demos? Devon: Two tests: reliability and scalability. A prototype might look magical on a dry stage in California, yet remain completely unviable in a rainy Scottish winter. By 2035, most cities will have quietly upgraded grid-scale storage and heat pumps—changes nobody films for social media, even though they lower bills and emissions every day. Nora: What about workplace automation? Are office roles bound to shrink? Devon: Routine data entry and basic scheduling may well shrink, yet demand for human judgement, troubleshooting, and clear explanation is unlikely to disappear. Ten years from now, doctors and engineers will be working alongside diagnostic software, checking edge cases and catching unforeseen errors. The smartest policy is building ethical safeguards and continuous adult retraining early, long before older systems become obsolete.

questions.prompt: What two tests does Devon say separate lasting breakthroughs from flashy demos?
options: Reliability in real conditions and scalability
High retail price and luxury design
questions.answer: Reliability in real conditions and scalability

questions.prompt: How does Devon expect workplace automation to affect skilled professionals by 2035?
options: They will work alongside tools while providing judgement and error checking
Human troubleshooting will become completely obsolete
questions.answer: They will work alongside tools while providing judgement and error checking

inputs.title: Why repairability may define the next decade of design
inputs.body: For much of the smartphone era, innovation was measured almost exclusively by speed, thinness, and annual upgrades. Consumers grew used to sealed batteries and glued screens that turned minor faults into expensive replacements, making perfectly functional hardware feel obsolete within three years. Today, however, a quiet shift is gaining momentum across engineering departments and European consumer law. Right-to-repair rules increasingly require manufacturers to supply spare parts, modular batteries, and plain repair manuals for years after a device leaves the shelf. By 2032, industry analysts estimate that major appliance makers will have redesigned most everyday electronics so local technicians can swap worn components in ten minutes rather than scrapping whole circuit boards. Critics once warned that modular design might slow down performance, yet early laptops built around replaceable ports and memory modules have proved commercially viable—and unexpectedly popular with universities and small businesses seeking predictable maintenance budgets. Admittedly, software automation and cloud tools will still tempt buyers toward newer models, and unforeseen supply bottlenecks can delay spare parts. Even so, durability is bound to become a genuine badge of prestige: the cleverest future device may not be the thinnest one on stage, but the one still running smoothly eight years later. Education systems and technical colleges are adjusting slowly to keep pace with this shift toward repairable, durable engineering. Instead of treating hardware purely as disposable consumer fashion, vocational programmes increasingly teach diagnostics, component replacement, and clean energy maintenance alongside coding. By the middle of the next decade, skilled repair technicians and systems auditors are likely to be among the most sought-after roles in local economies. If governments back clear labelling—showing expected battery lifespan and spare-part availability right beside the price—shoppers can reward thoughtful design with every ordinary purchase.

questions.prompt: What problem did sealed batteries and glued screens create?
options: Devices stayed in use for over ten years
Minor faults forced costly full replacements too early
Local repair shops ran out of customers
questions.answer: Minor faults forced costly full replacements too early

questions.prompt: Why have modular laptops appealed to universities and small businesses?
options: They offer easier repairs and more predictable maintenance budgets
They weigh twice as much as standard laptops
questions.answer: They offer easier repairs and more predictable maintenance budgets

modules.title: Persuasion and argument
modules.summary: Build persuasive B2 arguments using concession linkers (even though, despite, whereas) and consistent formal register.
modules.vocabularyTopic: Debate, evidence, concession and formal proposals

grammar.name: Linking devices and concession
grammar.explanation: Advanced writing needs linkers that signal contrast, consequence and concession precisely, with the right grammar after each one.
keyPoints: Contrast between clauses: Whereas the tax raised revenue, it hit low earners hardest.
Consequence: Consequently, consumption fell by eighteen per cent.
Concession: Nevertheless, the measure remains controversial. / In spite of the criticism, it stayed.
grammar.example: Whereas the levy reduced consumption, it was criticised as regressive; nevertheless, the government has kept it, in spite of two legal challenges.

items.prompt: ___ the tax raised revenue, it hit low earners hardest.
items.explanation: Whereas introduces a direct contrast between two clauses.

items.prompt: Consumption fell sharply; ___, revenue also dropped.
items.explanation: Consequently marks a result of the previous statement.

items.prompt: ___ the criticism, the policy remained in place.
items.explanation: In spite of + noun phrase expresses concession.

grammar.name: Formal register
grammar.explanation: Keep essays and proposals consistent by replacing conversational fillers, phrasal verbs, and contractions with precise academic or professional alternatives.
keyPoints: Replace "a lot of / big problem" with "a substantial proportion of / a pressing challenge".
Avoid contractions (don’t, can’t) and exclamation marks in formal proposals.
Choose formal verbs: "implement" instead of "put in place", "address" instead of "sort out".
grammar.example: Notwithstanding the initial capital cost, implementing flexible commuter passes would substantially ease rush-hour overcrowding.

items.prompt: ___ the initial cost, the pilot project delivered measurable savings within a year.
items.explanation: "Despite" takes a noun phrase ("the initial cost"), whereas "although" takes a clause.

items.prompt: Which sentence maintains consistent formal register for a council proposal?
options: We really should sort out this huge mess as soon as possible!
The committee should implement an independent review prior to renewing the contract.
Lots of folks reckon the current system doesn’t work at all.
items.answer: The committee should implement an independent review prior to renewing the contract.
items.explanation: Formal lexical choices without contractions or slang.

items.prompt: Public libraries cost relatively little to run, ___ their social return is substantial.
items.explanation: "Whereas" contrasts two full clauses cleanly.

inputs.title: How strong debaters concede without losing
inputs.body: Eleanor: Many B1 speakers worry that admitting any weakness in their own opinion ruins an argument. In reality, B2-level persuasion relies on doing the opposite: conceding a real point early so your rebuttal carries real weight. Liam, you coach university debating teams. What happens when a speaker refuses to acknowledge counter-arguments? Liam: Listeners immediately switch off because the argument feels one-sided and naive. Suppose you are arguing for a four-day working week. If you pretend every hospital or emergency service can simply close on Fridays, your credibility vanishes. Instead, a strong speaker says: "Admittedly, front-line services still require seven-day cover; nevertheless, administrative teams often maintain output in fewer hours when meetings are streamlined." Eleanor: And what about register in written proposals? Liam: In formal writing, small shifts make an immediate difference. Replacing "a lot of people hate" with "a significant proportion of residents object to" signals careful thought rather than personal frustration. Combining crisp linking devices—such as "despite", "whereas", and "consequently"—with one concrete piece of evidence turns loose opinions into compelling advocacy.

questions.prompt: Why does Liam say conceding an opponent’s point makes an argument stronger?
options: It shows balanced judgement and protects the speaker’s credibility
It fills extra speaking time without evidence
It confuses the audience about your position
questions.answer: It shows balanced judgement and protects the speaker’s credibility

questions.prompt: How should a speaker improve register in a formal written proposal?
options: Use precise wording and linking devices paired with concrete evidence
Write exactly as you chat with close friends
questions.answer: Use precise wording and linking devices paired with concrete evidence

inputs.title: How to write a proposal that gets read
inputs.body: Most proposals fail for a boring reason: the reader cannot find the recommendation. A useful proposal opens with the decision required, not with background. It states the problem in one paragraph, the options in three, and the recommendation in one sentence that could be quoted. Evidence should be proportionate: two strong figures persuade more than ten weak ones. Finally, anticipate the objection your reader will raise and answer it on the page, in their words. Not only does this show respect, but it also removes the easiest reason to say no. Look equally closely at how you rebut predictable objections. A persuasive proposal never waits for sceptical readers to raise budget or staffing worries in the margin; it anticipates the strongest counter-argument in paragraph three, concedes where compromises are sensible, and demonstrates why the remaining benefits still outweigh the drawbacks. Moreover, register consistency matters from the greeting to the closing recommendation. Mixing casual conversational idioms with stiff legal phrases makes a document read unevenly. Aim instead for clear, active formal prose: state the exact problem, cite one measurable outcome from a comparable pilot, specify who owns each action, and close with a realistic three-month review date. Readers remember proposals that respect their time and offer workable next steps. Finally, pay close attention to tone when finishing a formal argument. Ending with an exaggerated warning ("Otherwise, disaster is inevitable!") weakens hours of careful analysis, whereas a measured closing recommendation ("Implementing a six-month trial across two districts would test feasibility at modest cost") leaves decision-makers ready to engage. Strong persuasion rarely sounds aggressive; it combines respect for the reader’s intelligence with clear evidence, fair concessions, and an actionable path forward. Practising that calm authority prepares speakers and writers alike for university seminars, workplace proposals, and B2 assessments.

questions.prompt: What should a proposal open with?
What does the writer advise about evidence?

items.prompt: Even ___ clear evidence from pilot studies, several districts hesitated to act.
items.explanation: Concession before a noun phrase requires "despite" (or "in spite of").

items.prompt: Not only ___ reliable data crucial, but transparent communication also matters.
items.explanation: Negative inversion after "Not only" uses singular "is" to match uncountable "data" (treated singular here).

items.prompt: By next month, our cohort ___ completed sixteen weeks of structured output.
items.explanation: "By next month" calls for future perfect ("will have + past participle").

inputs.title: Timed listening: three accents, one topic
inputs.body: SPEAKER 1: I grew up in a city where nobody cycled, and now there are more bikes than cars on my old street. SPEAKER 2: The infrastructure came first, which is the opposite of what most cities try. You cannot ask people to change and then blame them when there is nowhere safe to go. SPEAKER 3: What interests me is the budget. Cycle lanes are cheap compared with a motorway, yet they are treated as a luxury. If the same money had gone into roads, nobody would have questioned it. In the second half of the seminar, the three speakers compared how learners move from comfortable B1 fluency into dependable B2 control. All three agreed that passive recognition is never enough: speaking and writing under gentle time pressure reveals exactly which grammar slips still appear automatically—whether missing articles, tense jumps, or awkward prepositions. Once a learner spots those two or three personal habits in an error log and practises rewriting them aloud, overall clarity jumps far faster than memorising rare idioms.

questions.answer: Cycle lanes are treated as a luxury

inputs.title: Timed reading: the limits of a good statistic
inputs.body: A single impressive number can end a discussion before it starts, which is precisely why it deserves suspicion. Take the claim that a policy 'created ten thousand jobs'. The figure may be accurate and still misleading: it says nothing about whether those jobs replaced others, how long they lasted, or who got them. Serious evaluation asks for the counterfactual — what would have happened anyway — and that is the question a headline rarely answers. Readers who learn to ask it become considerably harder to persuade with a number alone. Equally important at B2 level is knowing how to qualify a claim without sounding uncertain. Strong writers rarely announce that a policy "solves everything" or "fails completely"; instead, they explain the conditions under which evidence holds, acknowledge trade-offs openly, and cite realistic limits. Look closely at sample size, timeframe, and alternative explanations whenever a headline quotes a neat percentage. Developing that calm, analytical habit serves learners well whether they sit a formal B2 examination later or lead international discussions at work. Treating Checkpoint 4 as a snapshot of real progress—and naming one concrete next step if an area still needs polish—keeps long-term language growth grounded and motivating. Looking ahead after Week 16, maintaining B2 momentum requires far less daily effort than building it in the first place, provided output stays regular. Reading one longer feature article each weekend, listening to a varied mix of accents on your commute, and keeping a short personal notebook of awkward collocations ensures vocabulary keeps deepening naturally. Whenever a familiar tense or preposition slip reappears in writing, returning briefly to the Grammar Clinic keeps accuracy sharp. Above all, trust the cumulative effect of small, honest output: speaking and writing regularly turns hesitant knowledge into confident, lasting fluency.

options: They can be accurate yet misleading
questions.answer: They can be accurate yet misleading
